title: Anti-Defection Law

cards.b: Defection by legislators toppled governments in the 1960s and still does. The Tenth Schedule (1985) tried to stop it, and its working is still debated: does it protect stability or kill dissent? It is a core polity topic and often turns up in current affairs.

After the 1967 elections, over 400 defections occurred in states within a year. In Haryana, MLA Gaya Lal changed party three times in one day in 1967, giving us 'Aya Ram Gaya Ram'. The Chavan Committee (1968) studied it, and the Rajiv Gandhi government passed the 52nd Amendment in 1985, adding the Tenth Schedule.
Exceptions: merger of the original party if two-thirds of the legislature party agree (para 4), and the Speaker or Chairman resigning to stay neutral. Decisions are by the Presiding Officer.

The original law allowed a split if one-third members left. This led to mass defections, so the 91st Amendment removed the split provision and kept only the two-thirds merger. It also capped Councils of Ministers at 15 per cent of the House (minimum 12 in a state) and barred defectors from holding ministerial office or paid political posts until re-elected.

Kihoto Hollohan (1992) upheld the law, but held the Speaker's decision is a tribunal-like act and subject to judicial review (para 7, ouster of jurisdiction struck down). Rajendra Singh Rana (2007) on the Speaker's duty. Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020) urged Parliament to consider an independent tribunal and said Speakers should decide within three months. Subhash Desai (2023, Shiv Sena split) discussed whips and the Speaker's role.

cards.h: The whip and the free vote
cards.b: A whip is a party instruction on how to vote; a three-line whip is the strongest. Under the Tenth Schedule, defying it can cost a member the seat, though the party can condone it within 15 days. That makes legislators follow the party on every vote, not just on confidence. Burke's ideal of the representative as trustee exercising judgement fits badly. Parties may let members vote freely on conscience issues (a free vote). Related: Rajya Sabha elections now use an open ballot (2003 amendment to the RPA; Kuldip Nayar 2006) so that cross-voting can be traced.

• Speaker's partisanship: delay, selective action.
  • Whip applies to all votes, not only confidence motions: stifles free debate and the 'Burke trustee' ideal.
  • Merger loophole: whole groups (for example, Goa Congress MLAs in 2019 and 2022) merge with another party, and 'resort politics'.
  • Defectors often re-elected after resigning.

• Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) and the Law Commission (170th Report, 1999): limit disqualification to confidence and money votes.
  • Election Commission as decision-maker on Governor's advice (Goswami, Venkatachaliah 2002).
  • Second ARC: disqualification for confidence and budget votes.
  • Independent tribunal headed by a retired judge.
  • UK, Germany: no such law, party discipline by convention.

Defection reshaped Maharashtra (2022), Madhya Pradesh (2020), Karnataka (2019) and others. Elected members who change sides through resignation and by-election (the 'Operation Lotus' pattern) avoid disqualification. The debate links to party democracy, Speaker neutrality and the Rajya Sabha cross-voting rule (open ballot for party agents).
